newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani said to confess setting off bomb.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani said to confess setting off bomb.

text.p: Pakistani police said on Monday a Shi'ite Moslem activist had confessed to detonating a bomb that killed 26 people at the weekend in Lahore, including the leader of a militant Sunni Moslem group.
But the police did not allow reporters to question the suspect, Mehram Ali, a 35-year-old man, when they produced him briefly at a news conference.

Lahore's regional police chief, deputy inspector general Tariq Pervez, said Ali had confessed that he used a remote-control device to set off the bomb on Saturday outside a court in Lahore, capital of the central province of Punjab.

The Sunni Sipah-i-Sahaba Pakistan (SSP) group, which accuses Shi'ite militants for the bombing, on Monday called a general strike in the port city of Karachi to protest at the killing of its leader Zia-ur-Rahman Faruqi and 25 other people.

Deputy SSP leader Azam Tariq, one of about 90 people wounded in the blast, was released on parole from a Lahore hospital to attend the funeral prayers of his mother, who died of shock at the Punjab town of Chichawatni on Sunday, newspapers reported.
The bomb exploded as Faruqi and Tariq were being brought to the Sessions Court in Lahore, where they were due to appear on charges of involvement in murdering several Shi'ite Moslems.
Pervez said the suspect had told police that he had planned to kill Tariq, rather than Faruqi, because of his speeches attacking Shi'ite sect leaders.
He quoted Ali as saying he pushed the remote-control button from a distance of about 50 feet (15 metres).
Pervez said Ali had been arrested in 1990 and sentenced to 10 years in jail for possessing hand grenades but was later released by a higher court.
On Sunday, SSP activists sacked and burned the Iranian cultural centre in Lahore, drawing a protest from Tehran.
The Iranian foreign ministry on Sunday night summoned Pakistan's ambassador to Tehran and conveyed to him Iran's "strong protest" over the attack, Tehran radio said on Monday.

Iran also "seriously demanded that Pakistan's government deal with the perpetrators of the anti-Islamic act", the radio said. Several copies of the Koran were burnt and desecrated in the attack, the radio said.
Sunni hardliners blamed the bombing on largely Shi'ite Iran and the local Shi'ite group Tehrik-i-Jafria Pakistan.

No group has claimed responsibility. The attack appeared to be the latest in a long-running feud between militants in Pakistan's majority Sunni and minority Shi'ite communities, which cost about 170 lives last year.
Shi'ites form about 15 percent of Pakistan's population of over 130 million, but are a majority in neighbouring Iran.
Iran last week urged Pakistan to crack down on what it called terrorist groups and prevent killings of Shi'ites.
On Sunday, Pakistani newspapers quoted a spokesman from the Sunni group as saying that Iran was providing Shi'ite groups with guns and money. Iran has denied similar charges earlier.
